extracted.intended_audience: general readers, comedy fans, television researchers, and people interested in the Comedy Central Roast series
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptions and production/format standards for the Comedy Central Roast series: typical runtime, cast roles (roasters, roastmaster, roastee), content practices (off-limits topics, editing), and production/ratings details. Useful for understanding how these televised roasts are produced and moderated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series format and runtime
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy Central Roast is a series of celebrity roast specials; the network typically airs one or two roasts every year. Running time: 90 minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eight to ten people are invited, and they each roast one another before finally roasting the titular subject of the roast. Useful as a production/format standard when planning a roast special.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number and role of participants (roasters, roastmaster, roastee)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eight to ten roasters, plus a roastmaster who leads the event and a central roastee (the person being roasted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The roastmaster can be a recurring role; the page notes Seth MacFarlane as the most frequent roastmaster with three consecutive turns. Sometimes a previous roastmaster later becomes a roastee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roastee-specified off-limits topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Some roastees state that certain topics are off limits (examples: Pamela Anderson prohibited jokes about her Hepatitis C; Joan Rivers disallowed jokes about her daughter; William Shatner asked that the death of his wife not be mentioned).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other roastees have imposed no limits (example: David Hasselhoff). Even when initial agreement allows no restrictions, roastees may later request edits (example: Charlie Sheen asked that jokes about his mother be cut).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast editing and content removal
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes or segments are sometimes removed from the television broadcast for sensitivity, legal, or at-request reasons (examples: Steve-O's Station nightclub fire joke removed on request; Paul Walker jokes cut from Justin Bieber roast; Aurora massacre joke cut from Roseanne roast).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page documents multiple instances of material cut from the TV airing; DVD releases may differ (some sequences omitted from DVD or added back after being cut from broadcast).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-taped appearances and surprise guests
rubrics_metrics.description: Roasts commonly include pre-taped appearances and surprise guest appearances as part of the program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists many pre-taped and surprise guests across roasts; producers use pre-taped bits to supplement live roasts and include notable figures remotely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and acceptable comedic styles
rubrics_metrics.description: Roast humor is typically mean, racy, and insulting, targeting the roastee and fellow roasters; however, alternative tones are possible (example: Norm Macdonald's set avoided racy content and used intentionally cheesy and antiquated jokes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers and performers may vary tone—some sets are intentionally shocking, others deliberately tame or nostalgic—depending on performer style and show direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of montages and archival clips (and legal limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Roasts frequently include montages of the roastee's film/television work; legal limitations may prevent use of some clips (example: Charlie Sheen's Two and a Half Men clips were never used for legal reasons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers should clear rights for clips; omissions for legal reasons can shape the show's montage segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring roaster/credit expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain comedians recur frequently on Comedy Central Roasts (example: Jeff Ross has appeared in almost all roasts and is the most frequent roaster).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bringing recognized recurring roasters contributes to the roast's identity and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue and production location patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Roasts are filmed at specific venues; as of the Alec Baldwin roast, Sony Pictures Studios in Culver City hosted the most roasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing a venue familiar to the franchise (or suitable for television production) is part of production planning; the page lists common studios and venues used.

rubrics_metrics.name: International adaptations and local roasts
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 2010, Comedy Central affiliates outside the United States have occasionally produced their own roasts; multiple international roasts have aired in various countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local affiliates adapt the roast format for regional celebrities and audiences, which can change tone and content sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection, scheduling, and cancellation considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Planned roasts can be replaced or cancelled due to scheduling, production decisions, or conditions imposed by the roastee (example: Kid Rock's roast was cancelled because he wanted it filmed in Detroit, a condition Comedy Central refused).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negotiations over location, scheduling, and format can determine whether a roast proceeds; network priorities and logistics influence selections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity to tragedies and removal of jokes referencing deaths
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes referencing real tragedies, deaths, or sensitive events are frequently removed from the broadcast (examples: Station nightclub fire reference removed; jokes about Paul Walker cut).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers and editors exercise caution with material that recalls recent or traumatic events; removal may be done proactively or upon request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience reaction, editing for perception, and reputation management
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing can be used to manage how performers and sets appear to the television audience (example: Jeff Ross stated they edited Ann Coulter's set 'to make her look as best we could'; Coulter claimed editing made her look like she bombed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers may shape the televised narrative through selective editing; performers and subjects should be aware the aired version may differ significantly from the live show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratings and viewership as success metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Television viewership numbers are tracked and cited (examples: Denis Leary roast 3.2 million viewers; Charlie Sheen roast 6.4 million, the highest to date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ratings are used to assess a roast's commercial success and may influence future booking and production choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age and legal/ethical considerations for roastees
rubrics_metrics.description: Age of the roastee can be notable (example: Justin Bieber at 21 was the youngest Comedy Central roastee to date) and may influence content choices and public reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers should consider age and associated sensibilities or legal constraints when approving material and edits.
